subject: anatomy
title: Front, medial and back of thigh: key anatomy for exams

steps.tx: The thigh has three compartments. The **anterior** compartment holds the quadriceps and is supplied by the femoral nerve. The **medial** compartment holds the adductors and is supplied by the obturator nerve. The **posterior** compartment holds the hamstrings and is supplied by the sciatic nerve. Adductor magnus is the exception, with a dual supply from the obturator and sciatic nerves. Learn this compartment-nerve pairing first, because most exam questions test it.
steps.say: The thigh has three compartments. The anterior compartment holds the quadriceps and is supplied by the femoral nerve. The medial compartment holds the adductors and is supplied by the obturator nerve. The posterior compartment holds the hamstrings and is supplied by the sciatic nerve. Adductor magnus is the exception, with a dual supply from the obturator and sciatic nerves. Learn this pairing first, because most exam questions test it.

steps.tx: The femoral triangle lies below the inguinal ligament. From lateral to medial it contains the **femoral nerve**, the **femoral artery** and the **femoral vein**, with the lymphatics and femoral canal most medial. The femoral sheath is a funnel of fascia around the upper 3 to 4 cm of the femoral vessels. Its medial compartment is the **femoral canal**, which is the site of femoral hernia. The femoral vein lies lateral to the femoral canal, so it is the structure that sits next to the hernia sac on that side.
steps.say: The femoral triangle lies below the inguinal ligament. From lateral to medial it contains the femoral nerve, the femoral artery and the femoral vein, with the lymphatics and femoral canal most medial. The femoral sheath is a funnel of fascia around the upper three to four centimetres of the femoral vessels. Its medial compartment is the femoral canal, which is the site of femoral hernia. The femoral vein lies lateral to the femoral canal.

Medial: femoral canal with lymph node of Cloquet

steps.tx: The adductor canal, also called Hunter's or subsartorial canal, lies in the medial middle third of the thigh. It is triangular in cross section. Its roof is formed by a fibrous membrane under the **sartorius**, and its floor is adductor longus above and adductor magnus below. Its contents are the femoral artery, the femoral vein, the **saphenous nerve** and the nerve to vastus medialis. The nerve to vastus lateralis is not a content, which is a common exam trap.
steps.say: The adductor canal, also called Hunter's or subsartorial canal, lies in the medial middle third of the thigh. It is triangular in cross section. Its roof is a fibrous membrane under sartorius, and its floor is adductor longus above and adductor magnus below. Its contents are the femoral artery, the femoral vein, the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis. The nerve to vastus lateralis is not a content.

steps.tx: The **profunda femoris** is the largest branch of the femoral artery. It arises about 4 cm below the inguinal ligament and supplies all three thigh compartments. Its medial circumflex femoral branch supplies most of the femoral head. Some posterior thigh supply also comes from the inferior gluteal artery above and the popliteal artery below. The **cruciate anastomosis** links the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries with the gluteal vessels, and is a key collateral route in femoral neck fracture.
steps.say: The profunda femoris is the largest branch of the femoral artery. It arises about four centimetres below the inguinal ligament and supplies all three thigh compartments. Its medial circumflex femoral branch supplies most of the femoral head. The cruciate anastomosis links circumflex and gluteal vessels and acts as a collateral route.

vis.alt: Branching diagram of the profunda femoris artery: arises about 4 cm below the inguinal ligament and gives medial circumflex femoral, lateral circumflex femoral and four perforating arteries, supplying all three thigh compartments.
vis.caption: Profunda femoris is the main artery of the thigh; its perforators supply the posterior compartment.

steps.tx: The **great saphenous vein** is the usual site of venous cut down. The **saphenous nerve**, a branch of the femoral nerve, runs with it and can be damaged during that procedure. The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh arises from L2 and L3 and supplies the lateral thigh, so it is not the answer for medial thigh skin. For India, NEET-PG and INI-CET, and for USMLE, these anatomy patterns are tested repeatedly.
steps.say: The great saphenous vein is the usual site of venous cut down. The saphenous nerve, a branch of the femoral nerve, runs with it and can be damaged during that procedure. The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh supplies the lateral thigh, not the medial side.

vis.alt: Diagram of the great saphenous vein: starts in front of the medial malleolus, ascends the medial leg and thigh with the saphenous nerve, and enters the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction after receiving superficial tributaries.
vis.caption: The saphenous nerve travels with the vein below the knee, which is why cut-down can injure it.
